slides.heading: The Hidden World of Microplastics
slides.body: Tiny plastic particles are everywhere — including inside you. Here's what science says.

slides.heading: What Are Microplastics?
slides.body: Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than 5mm — many invisible to the naked eye. They form when larger plastics break down from UV light, heat, and mechanical wear. Nanoplastics, under 1 micrometer, can penetrate cells directly.

slides.heading: They're Literally Everywhere
slides.body: Scientists have found microplastics in the deepest ocean trenches, the highest mountain peaks, and in Antarctic ice. A 2023 study detected them in every human blood sample tested. There is no pristine place on Earth left.

slides.heading: How They Enter Your Body
slides.body: You ingest microplastics through food, drinking water, and even the air you breathe. Seafood, bottled water, and sea salt are major dietary sources. Studies estimate humans consume up to a credit card's worth of plastic per week.

slides.heading: Inside the Human Body
slides.body: Researchers have found microplastics in human lungs, liver, kidneys, placenta, and breast milk. A landmark 2024 study found them embedded in arterial plaque, linking higher concentrations to greater risk of heart attack and stroke.

slides.heading: The Health Concerns
slides.body: Microplastics carry harmful chemicals — including endocrine disruptors and carcinogens — that can leach into tissues. They also act as carriers for pathogens and heavy metals. Long-term health effects are still being studied, but early signals are alarming.

slides.heading: Damage to Ecosystems
slides.body: Marine animals mistake microplastics for food, leading to starvation and chemical poisoning. They disrupt plankton — Earth's primary oxygen producers and CO2 absorbers. Microplastic pollution is now considered a planetary boundary threat.

slides.heading: Where Do They Come From?
slides.body: Single-use packaging, synthetic textiles, and vehicle tires are the top sources. A single laundry cycle releases up to 700,000 microfibers. Road runoff from tire wear is now one of the largest sources entering waterways.

slides.heading: What Can Be Done?
slides.body: Filtering washing machine wastewater, reducing single-use plastics, and switching to natural fibers all help. New biodegradable polymers and advanced water filtration are promising. Policy solutions like extended producer responsibility laws are gaining traction globally.

slides.heading: A Plastic Planet Needs Plastic-Free Thinking
slides.body: Microplastics are the pollution we cannot see but cannot ignore. Individual choices matter — but systemic change is essential to protect human health and the planet.
